options.text: alveolar O2 rises to a toxic level

options.label: B
options.text: the cortex loses control of the diaphragm

options.label: C
options.text: rising CO2 and falling O2 force a breath

options.label: D
options.text: the lungs collapse once the residual volume is reached

options.label: E
options.text: the pneumotaxic centre is fatigued

questions.why: During voluntary breath-holding, ongoing metabolism consumes oxygen and produces carbon dioxide without alveolar ventilation. Rising carbon dioxide, increasing acidity and eventually falling oxygen intensify involuntary respiratory drive, contributing to the breakpoint at which voluntary suppression becomes difficult.

notes.A: Alveolar oxygen generally falls during breath-holding as metabolism continues, rather than rising towards a toxic oxygen partial pressure.
notes.B: Voluntary cortical control can initially suppress breathing despite increasing respiratory drive; the breakpoint reflects mounting chemical and respiratory motor influences rather than isolated cortical failure.
notes.D: Residual volume is the gas remaining after maximal expiration, and the urge to breathe is not normally caused by mechanical lung collapse at that volume.
notes.E: Pontine circuits contribute to breathing pattern control, but their fatigue is not the principal established explanation for the voluntary breath-holding breakpoint.

questions.stem: Giving a very low concentration of oxygen raises ventilation only weakly because the hyperventilation it causes

options.label: A
options.text: fatigues the carotid bodies within seconds

options.label: B
options.text: shifts the dissociation curve to the left

options.label: C
options.text: directly excites the pneumotaxic centre

options.label: D
options.text: washing out CO2, which inhibits breathing

options.label: E
options.text: at once raises arterial O2 back to normal

questions.why: Hypoxic hyperventilation blows off CO2; the hypocapnia opposes the drive, so only a very low PO2 overrides it.

questions.stem: In a patient with chronic CO2 retention whose drive to breathe has become dependent on hypoxia, the danger of giving 100% oxygen is that it may

options.label: A
options.text: cause an immediate respiratory alkalosis

options.label: B
options.text: trigger bronchospasm through cold air

options.label: C
options.text: precipitate carbon monoxide poisoning

options.label: D
options.text: shift the oxygen curve far to the right

options.label: E
options.text: remove the hypoxic drive and depress ventilation

questions.why: When the CO2 response is blunted, hypoxia is the main stimulus; abolishing it with high O2 can depress breathing.

questions.stem: The cough reflex is initiated by touch-sensitive receptors in the bronchi and trachea whose afferents travel in the

options.label: A
options.text: vagus nerve

options.label: B
options.text: glossopharyngeal nerve

options.label: C
options.text: trigeminal nerve

options.label: D
options.text: phrenic nerve

options.label: E
options.text: facial nerve

questions.why: Mechanical and chemical stimulation of sensory endings in the larynx, trachea and bronchi can activate vagal afferent pathways to brainstem cough networks. Coordinated respiratory and laryngeal muscle activity then produces forceful expiratory airflow to clear the airway.

notes.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries pharyngeal sensory information and carotid body signals, rather than the principal tracheobronchial cough afferent pathway.
notes.C: The trigeminal nerve conveys nasal sensory signals important for sneezing, whereas lower-airway cough receptors predominantly communicate through vagal afferents.
notes.D: The phrenic nerve activates the diaphragm during respiratory movements, but the principal sensory trigger for tracheobronchial cough travels through the vagus.
notes.E: The facial nerve supplies muscles of facial expression and selected secretory pathways, rather than carrying the main lower-airway cough receptor signals.

questions.stem: The sneeze reflex resembles the cough reflex but is triggered through the ___ nerve and directs air through the nose by depressing the uvula.

options.label: A
options.text: accessory

options.label: B
options.text: trigeminal

options.label: C
options.text: vagus

options.label: D
options.text: glossopharyngeal

options.label: E
options.text: hypoglossal

questions.why: Nasal mucosal irritation activates sensory fibres of the trigeminal nerve, which convey signals to brainstem sneeze-generating networks. The coordinated respiratory and upper-airway motor response produces rapid expulsive airflow through the nose and often the mouth.

notes.A: The accessory nerve chiefly supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, rather than transmitting the nasal mucosal sensory signals that trigger sneezing.
notes.C: Vagal afferents play a major role in cough initiated from the larynx and lower airways, whereas nasal irritation primarily uses trigeminal afferents.
notes.D: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies sensory pathways from the pharynx and carotid region, rather than the principal sensory innervation of nasal mucosa.
notes.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies tongue muscles and may participate indirectly in airway positioning, but does not carry the sensory trigger from nasal irritation.

questions.stem: In the standard classification of hypoxia, 'anaemic hypoxia' means that

options.label: A
options.text: a toxin blocks the tissue's use of O2

options.label: B
options.text: oxygen cannot diffuse across the alveolar membrane

options.label: C
options.text: there is too little functional haemoglobin to carry O2

options.label: D
options.text: the arterial PO2 itself is reduced

options.label: E
options.text: blood flow to the tissue is too slow

questions.why: Anaemic hypoxia occurs when arterial blood has inadequate oxygen-carrying capacity because the amount of functional haemoglobin is reduced. Arterial oxygen partial pressure can remain normal because it measures dissolved oxygen rather than total haemoglobin-bound oxygen content.

notes.A: Failure of tissues to utilise available oxygen, as in cyanide poisoning, defines histotoxic rather than anaemic hypoxia.
notes.B: Impaired alveolar gas transfer can lower arterial oxygen tension and produce hypoxaemic hypoxia, rather than a primary reduction in functional haemoglobin.
notes.D: Reduced arterial oxygen partial pressure characterises hypoxaemic hypoxia; anaemic hypoxia can occur with normal arterial oxygen tension.
notes.E: Inadequate blood flow limits oxygen delivery despite potentially normal arterial oxygen content, producing circulatory or stagnant rather than anaemic hypoxia.

questions.stem: Cyanide poisoning produces which type of hypoxia?

options.label: A
options.text: anaemic hypoxia

options.label: B
options.text: stagnant hypoxia

options.label: C
options.text: anaemic hypoxia from CO

options.label: D
options.text: histotoxic hypoxia

options.label: E
options.text: hypoxic hypoxia

questions.why: Cyanide inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase, impairing the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation. Oxygen may be delivered adequately to tissues but cannot be utilised normally, producing histotoxic hypoxia and potentially increased venous oxygen content.

notes.A: Anaemic hypoxia results primarily from reduced effective haemoglobin oxygen-carrying capacity, rather than inhibition of cellular mitochondrial oxygen utilisation.
notes.B: Stagnant hypoxia arises from inadequate blood flow and oxygen delivery; cyanide instead disrupts oxygen use even when perfusion is initially maintained.
notes.C: Carbon monoxide principally impairs oxygen carriage and unloading through haemoglobin binding, whereas cyanide chiefly inhibits mitochondrial oxidative metabolism.
notes.E: Hypoxaemic hypoxia involves reduced arterial oxygen partial pressure, whereas cyanide poisoning can impair cellular oxygen use despite adequate arterial oxygen tension.

questions.stem: Slow blood flow, as in shock or heart failure, causes which type of hypoxia?

options.label: A
options.text: histotoxic hypoxia

options.label: B
options.text: hypoxic hypoxia

options.label: C
options.text: anaemic hypoxia

options.label: D
options.text: diffusion hypoxia

options.label: E
options.text: stagnant hypoxia

questions.why: Stagnant or circulatory hypoxia results from insufficient tissue blood flow relative to metabolic demand. Oxygen delivery decreases because flow is reduced, even when arterial oxygen tension and haemoglobin oxygen content are initially adequate; tissues may compensate by extracting more oxygen.

notes.A: Histotoxic hypoxia involves impaired cellular oxygen utilisation, whereas stagnant hypoxia is caused principally by inadequate perfusion and oxygen delivery.
notes.B: Hypoxaemic hypoxia results from reduced arterial oxygen partial pressure; slow-flow hypoxia can occur even with normal arterial oxygen tension.
notes.C: Anaemic hypoxia is caused by inadequate functional haemoglobin and reduced blood oxygen-carrying capacity rather than a primary fall in tissue perfusion.
notes.D: Diffusion-related oxygen impairment involves resistance to gas transfer, whereas shock-related slow-flow hypoxia primarily reflects reduced delivery of blood to tissues.

questions.stem: Clinically detectable cyanosis generally appears once the concentration of reduced (deoxygenated) haemoglobin reaches about

options.label: A
options.text: 5 g/dl

options.label: B
options.text: 1 g/dl

options.label: C
options.text: 10 g/dl

options.label: D
options.text: 15 g/dl

options.label: E
options.text: 2 g/dl

questions.why: Classical clinical teaching associates visible cyanosis with approximately 5 g/dL of reduced haemoglobin in capillary blood. This is an approximate historical threshold rather than a fixed diagnostic rule, because lighting, pigmentation, perfusion and total haemoglobin influence visibility.

notes.B: One gram per decilitre is below the conventional historical reduced-haemoglobin threshold, although cyanosis detection varies considerably with clinical circumstances.
notes.C: Ten grams per decilitre of reduced haemoglobin would represent substantial deoxygenation and exceeds the traditional teaching estimate for cyanosis becoming visible.
notes.D: Fifteen grams per decilitre approaches the entire haemoglobin concentration of many healthy adults and is much higher than the classical visibility threshold.
notes.E: Two grams per decilitre is below the conventional five-gram teaching threshold, although actual clinical detection is variable and cannot be assessed from this value alone.

questions.stem: Severe anaemia rarely shows cyanosis even when the patient is hypoxic because

options.label: A
options.text: methaemoglobin masks the colour

options.label: B
options.text: too little Hb to give 5 g/dl of reduced Hb

options.label: C
options.text: the remaining haemoglobin is cherry red

options.label: D
options.text: arterial O2 is actually increased

options.label: E
options.text: the skin vessels are maximally dilated

questions.why: Cyanosis depends on the absolute amount of reduced haemoglobin rather than oxygen saturation alone. Severe anaemia reduces total haemoglobin, so even substantial desaturation may produce little visible cyanosis; absence of cyanosis cannot exclude inadequate oxygen delivery.

notes.A: Methaemoglobin can itself produce abnormal bluish discoloration and impaired oxygen carriage, rather than generally masking cyanosis specifically in severe anaemia.
notes.C: Cherry-red discoloration is classically associated with carboxyhaemoglobin and is not the usual explanation for reduced cyanosis in patients with low total haemoglobin.
notes.D: Anaemia reduces oxygen content despite potentially normal arterial oxygen tension; an increase in arterial oxygen tension is not required to explain absent cyanosis.
notes.E: Skin perfusion influences the appearance of peripheral cyanosis, but reduced absolute haemoglobin concentration is the principal explanation in severe anaemia.

questions.stem: On rapid ascent to high altitude, the earliest compensatory response to the low inspired PO2 is

options.label: A
options.text: a fall in plasma pH from lactic acid

options.label: B
options.text: immediate polycythaemia

options.label: C
options.text: hyperventilation from chemoreceptor drive

options.label: D
options.text: a rise in red cell mass from erythropoietin

options.label: E
options.text: an increase in 2,3-DPG within hours

questions.why: A rapid ascent lowers barometric pressure and inspired oxygen partial pressure, reducing arterial oxygen tension. Peripheral chemoreceptors, especially the carotid bodies, promptly stimulate hyperventilation, improving alveolar oxygen tension before slower haematological and renal adaptations develop.

notes.A: The immediate hyperventilatory response commonly lowers arterial carbon dioxide and raises pH, rather than necessarily producing primary lactic acidaemia.
notes.B: An immediate increase in red-cell mass is impossible through new erythrocyte production; early haemoconcentration may occur later with plasma volume changes.
notes.D: Hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin, but expansion of red-cell mass requires erythropoiesis over subsequent days to weeks, not the earliest respiratory compensation.
notes.E: Changes in erythrocyte 2,3-DPG can develop during acclimatisation, but peripheral chemoreceptor-driven ventilation increases much more rapidly after ascent.

questions.stem: Over several days of acclimatization to altitude, a rise in 2,3-DPG is useful because it

options.label: A
options.text: raises the plasma bicarbonate directly

options.label: B
options.text: suppresses erythropoietin secretion

options.label: C
options.text: reduces the ventilatory response to hypoxia

options.label: D
options.text: shifts the curve rightward, making O2 more available to tissues

options.label: E
options.text: shifts the curve leftward, loading more O2 in the lungs

questions.why: Altitude acclimatisation can increase erythrocyte 2,3-DPG, stabilising deoxygenated haemoglobin and tending to shift the oxygen dissociation curve rightwards. This can facilitate tissue oxygen unloading, although concurrent respiratory alkalosis exerts an opposing leftward effect.

notes.A: 2,3-DPG is an erythrocyte glycolytic intermediate regulating haemoglobin affinity, rather than a direct mechanism increasing plasma bicarbonate concentration.
notes.B: Erythropoietin secretion is regulated principally by renal oxygen sensing, not by a direct inhibitory action of erythrocyte 2,3-DPG.
notes.C: The ventilatory response to altitude is influenced by chemoreceptors and acid–base adaptation, rather than directly suppressed by an increase in haemoglobin-bound 2,3-DPG.
notes.E: Increased 2,3-DPG tends to decrease haemoglobin oxygen affinity and shift its curve rightwards, rather than enhancing affinity through a leftward shift.

questions.stem: Erythropoietin released during acclimatization to altitude acts to

options.label: A
options.text: increase 2,3-DPG within minutes

options.label: B
options.text: stimulate the respiratory centre directly

options.label: C
options.text: cause immediate bronchodilatation

options.label: D
options.text: reduce plasma volume acutely

options.label: E
options.text: raise haemoglobin and red cell mass over a few days

questions.why: EPO rises with hypoxia and increases haemoglobin over 2–3 days, a key part of acclimatization.

questions.stem: Acute mountain sickness some hours after arrival at altitude is attributed partly to arteriolar dilatation that raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and causes

options.label: A
options.text: cerebral and pulmonary oedema

options.label: B
options.text: bronchospasm and wheeze

options.label: C
options.text: methaemoglobinaemia

options.label: D
options.text: decompression bubbles in the joints

options.label: E
options.text: haemolysis of red cells

questions.why: Hypoxic arteriolar dilatation raises capillary pressure, leaking fluid into brain and lung — cerebral and pulmonary oedema.

questions.stem: In a diver breathing compressed air, the narcotic effect producing euphoria and impaired judgement at depth is due to raised

options.label: A
options.text: water vapour pressure

options.label: B
options.text: nitrogen partial pressure

options.label: C
options.text: oxygen partial pressure

options.label: D
options.text: carbon dioxide partial pressure

options.label: E
options.text: helium partial pressure

questions.why: At increased ambient pressure, the partial pressure of inhaled nitrogen rises when breathing compressed air. Elevated nitrogen tension has reversible narcotic effects on the central nervous system, potentially impairing judgement, coordination and awareness during deep diving.

notes.A: Water vapour pressure is largely determined by temperature in humidified airways, rather than the inert-gas partial-pressure increase responsible for nitrogen narcosis.
notes.C: High oxygen partial pressure can cause oxygen toxicity, including neurological manifestations, but classic inert-gas narcosis while breathing compressed air is chiefly nitrogen-related.
notes.D: Carbon dioxide retention can impair cognition and worsen diving hazards, but it is not the defining inert-gas mechanism of nitrogen narcosis.
notes.E: Helium has substantially less narcotic potency than nitrogen at comparable pressures and is used in some breathing mixtures to reduce nitrogen-related narcosis.

questions.stem: Decompression sickness ('the bends') on rapid ascent from a deep dive is caused by

options.label: A
options.text: rupture of alveoli from over-expansion

options.label: B
options.text: cold-induced bronchospasm

options.label: C
options.text: nitrogen bubbles coming out of solution

options.label: D
options.text: oxygen toxicity damaging the lungs

options.label: E
options.text: carbon dioxide retention in muscle

questions.why: At elevated ambient pressure, more inert nitrogen can dissolve in body tissues. If pressure decreases too rapidly, supersaturation can cause gas bubbles to form in tissues and blood, producing decompression sickness with musculoskeletal, neurological or other manifestations.

notes.A: Alveolar overexpansion during ascent can cause pulmonary barotrauma and arterial gas embolism, which are distinct from decompression sickness caused by dissolved inert gas.
notes.B: Cold-induced bronchospasm narrows airways and may complicate diving, but does not produce the systemic inert-gas bubble mechanism of decompression sickness.
notes.D: Oxygen toxicity results from excessive oxygen partial pressure and oxidative injury, rather than nitrogen supersaturation during a decrease in ambient pressure.
notes.E: Carbon dioxide retention can cause hypercapnia and impair performance, but decompression sickness specifically involves bubbles arising from dissolved inert gases.

questions.stem: Breathing 100% oxygen for many hours is harmful partly because it

options.label: A
options.text: causes immediate nitrogen narcosis

options.label: B
options.text: raises plasma bicarbonate sharply

options.label: C
options.text: triggers the Hering-Breuer reflex

options.label: D
options.text: inhibits surfactant production and injures the airway

options.label: E
options.text: shifts the dissociation curve far to the right

questions.why: Prolonged exposure to excessively high oxygen concentrations can generate reactive oxygen species that injure pulmonary epithelial and endothelial cells. Inflammation, impaired surfactant function and altered alveolar–capillary barrier integrity can reduce lung compliance and gas-exchange efficiency.

notes.A: Nitrogen narcosis results from high nitrogen partial pressure at depth, rather than prolonged exposure to pure oxygen under ordinary ambient pressure.
notes.B: High inspired oxygen does not characteristically cause a sharp primary increase in plasma bicarbonate; pulmonary oxygen toxicity principally reflects oxidative tissue injury.
notes.C: The Hering–Breuer inflation reflex responds to mechanical lung stretch, rather than being the mechanism of tissue injury during prolonged oxygen exposure.
notes.E: Oxygen toxicity does not primarily result from a rightward haemoglobin affinity shift; excessive oxygen tension instead promotes oxidant-mediated cellular damage.

questions.stem: In a premature infant, prolonged high-concentration oxygen therapy can cause the eye complication

options.label: A
options.text: cataract from lens opacification

options.label: B
options.text: optic neuritis

options.label: C
options.text: central retinal artery occlusion

options.label: D
options.text: glaucoma

options.label: E
options.text: retrolental fibroplasia

questions.why: Excessive or poorly controlled oxygen exposure in premature infants can disrupt normal retinal vascular development, contributing to retinopathy of prematurity. Advanced disease may involve fibrovascular proliferation and retinal detachment, historically described as retrolental fibroplasia.

notes.A: Cataracts involve lens opacity, whereas the characteristic oxygen-associated complication in premature infants principally affects developing retinal blood vessels.
notes.B: Optic neuritis is inflammation of the optic nerve and is not the characteristic developmental retinal vascular disorder associated with premature-infant oxygen exposure.
notes.C: Central retinal artery occlusion causes acute retinal ischaemia, rather than the abnormal developmental vascular proliferation characteristic of retinopathy of prematurity.
notes.D: Glaucoma involves optic neuropathy often associated with elevated intraocular pressure, rather than the characteristic oxygen-associated disorder of immature retinal vasculature.

questions.stem: During exercise the venous PO2 falls (for example from 40 toward 25 mmHg), which aids oxygenation in the lungs by

options.label: A
options.text: a wider alveolar-to-capillary O2 gradient

options.label: B
options.text: reducing the diffusing capacity of the membrane

options.label: C
options.text: raising alveolar PCO2 above arterial PCO2

options.label: D
options.text: closing dormant pulmonary capillaries

options.label: E
options.text: shifting the dissociation curve to the left

questions.why: During exercise, greater tissue oxygen extraction lowers mixed venous oxygen tension entering pulmonary capillaries. The larger initial alveolar-to-capillary oxygen gradient favours diffusion, while capillary recruitment and distension also increase pulmonary diffusing capacity to accommodate increased blood flow.

notes.B: Pulmonary diffusing capacity usually increases during exercise through capillary recruitment and distension, rather than decreasing as mixed venous oxygen tension falls.
notes.C: The widened oxygen gradient concerns alveolar and incoming venous oxygen tensions; an increase in alveolar carbon dioxide above arterial values is not required.
notes.D: Exercise commonly recruits previously underperfused pulmonary capillaries and distends open vessels, increasing rather than reducing the effective gas-exchange area.
notes.E: The exercise-associated rise in temperature and acidity generally favours a rightward oxygen affinity shift, rather than explaining pulmonary uptake through a leftward shift.

questions.stem: In severe exercise an added chemical stimulus to the respiratory centre is

options.label: A
options.text: an increase in plasma bicarbonate

options.label: B
options.text: lactic acid that liberates CO2

options.label: C
options.text: a rise in arterial oxygen tension

options.label: D
options.text: a fall in core body temperature

options.label: E
options.text: a rise in red-cell 2,3-DPG alone

questions.why: During strenuous exercise, increased glycolytic acid production can increase hydrogen ion concentration. Bicarbonate buffering generates additional carbon dioxide, while peripheral chemoreceptor stimulation by acidaemia contributes to the disproportionately increased ventilation seen above the ventilatory threshold.

notes.A: Bicarbonate is consumed when buffering excess metabolic hydrogen ions, rather than its increase providing the additional characteristic stimulus during heavy exercise.
notes.C: Arterial oxygen tension is often maintained during exercise, and an increase in oxygen tension would not provide the usual hypoxic ventilatory stimulus.
notes.D: Core temperature generally rises during strenuous exercise; a fall in temperature is not the characteristic additional chemical stimulus associated with exercise acidosis.
notes.E: 2,3-DPG modifies haemoglobin oxygen affinity, but does not directly explain the additional ventilatory drive from metabolic acidaemia during strenuous exercise.

questions.stem: A victim of fresh-water (hypotonic) near-drowning is at particular risk of

options.label: A
options.text: nitrogen narcosis

options.label: B
options.text: carbon monoxide poisoning

options.label: C
options.text: intravascular haemolysis of red cells

options.label: D
options.text: loss of plasma into the lungs causing shock

options.label: E
options.text: immediate decompression sickness

questions.why: Hypotonic fresh water is absorbed into the circulation and lyses red cells; sea water instead draws plasma into the lungs.

questions.stem: Hypocapnia from voluntary hyperventilation can cause tetany because the accompanying respiratory alkalosis

options.label: A
options.text: increases arterial PCO2

options.label: B
options.text: depresses the respiratory centre immediately

options.label: C
options.text: shifts the oxygen curve to the right

options.label: D
options.text: lowers ionised plasma calcium

options.label: E
options.text: raises ionised plasma calcium

questions.why: Hyperventilation lowers arterial carbon dioxide tension and raises blood pH, producing respiratory alkalosis. Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin, reducing the physiologically active ionised calcium fraction and increasing neuromuscular excitability, which may cause paraesthesiae or tetany.

notes.A: Increased ventilation removes carbon dioxide faster, lowering rather than raising arterial carbon dioxide tension during acute voluntary hyperventilation.
notes.B: Hypocapnia can reduce respiratory drive, but that feedback does not directly explain the increased neuromuscular excitability associated with alkalosis-induced tetany.
notes.C: Reduced carbon dioxide and increased pH favour a leftward oxygen dissociation-curve shift; calcium binding changes instead explain the characteristic tetany.
notes.E: Alkalosis generally decreases ionised calcium by increasing its protein binding, even when total plasma calcium concentration remains essentially unchanged.

questions.stem: Asphyxia from airway occlusion combines low O2 with high CO2 and characteristically causes an early

options.label: A
options.text: fall in blood pressure with bradycardia

options.label: B
options.text: respiratory alkalosis

options.label: C
options.text: immediate loss of chemoreceptor activity

options.label: D
options.text: fall in circulating catecholamines

options.label: E
options.text: raised blood pressure and heart rate

questions.why: Asphyxia strongly drives respiration and sympathetic output, raising BP, heart rate and catecholamines before eventual collapse.
